newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW-Compaq plans ambitious push in Japan.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Compaq plans ambitious push in Japan.

text.p: Compaq Computer Corp, the world's top seller of personal computers, says it plans an ambitious push to increase its market share in Japan where it has been struggling to compete.
It said it will increase its work force by nearly 40 percent at its Japanese unit by the end of the year in a bid to inject some energy into its business here.

"We want to hire 120 new workers this year. A little over 60 in our marketing section and about 50 more mainly in technical service," Kuniaki Fujimoto, president of Compaq's Japanese unit, Compaq KK, told Reuters in a recent interview.
Fujimoto said the planned hirings -- the firm currently has 315 employees -- reflect the firm's desire to boost revenues and profits, but he declined to provide specific target figures.

Compaq, which has captured more than 11 percent of the global PC market, has struggled to duplicate that success in Japan, where last year it ranked seventh with three percent of the market, which was down one percentage point from 1995.
Fujimoto, who took over the helm of Compaq KK in March, has said he wants to raise Compaq's share of the Japanese market to around 10 percent in the short term.
Fujimoto said a major source of revenue will come from the sale of client-server systems, in contrast to previously emphasising the sale of low-priced PCs.

When Compaq first entered Japan in 1992 with its PCs, it created the so-called "Compaq Shock", and triggered fierce price competition with its low-priced PCs costing about 50 percent less than those offered by Japanese competitors.
But it failed to to make much of a dent, trailing far behind top seller NEC Corp, which had a 33 percent market share in 1996, and the second-ranked Fujitsu Ltd, which had 22 percent.
"Compaq lacked a good strategy for using local marketing channels," said Katsushi Shiga, an analyst at market research firm Dataquest.
He said Compaq did not offer enough incentives to wholesalers to sell its computers. "Japanese PC makers provide their wholesalers with a much larger margin than Compaq," he said.

Shiga also said that Japanese PC makers traditionally have a strong hold on the domestic market because many corporate clients lack sufficient knowledge about computers and depend on the makers to make decisions.

Katsuichi Tomita, a vice president at NEC Corp, said Compaq's weakness lay in relying too much on its low prices, instead of providing customer services, including after-sales care and computer lessons.
"Compaq's success in the United States does not necessary mean that it can be repeated in Japan," Tomita said.
However, Fujimoto said he is confident the planned changes will put Compaq on a rapid growth track.
The company has already implemented on a new assessment and incentive programme for its workers.
Fujimoto also said Compaq planned to begin offering a build-to-order service later this year, depending on how it does in the United States, where it is to be introduced sometime this year.
The service will enable Compaq to respond more quickly to corporate orders and reduce inventory costs, he said.
